sweep_summary: The single works with stress in the title (Feng 2016, 'Hanyu yulü yufa wenda') is a book on Mandarin Chinese prosodic grammar that Glottolog mis-assigned to Yulu-Binga by a computerised string match on 'yulu' (the record says so explicitly); relevance other-language, priority none. To make this search of works with stress in the title useful I downloaded the three open HAL manuscripts by Boyeldieu not yet held by the project (2007 Compound Verbs, the catalog's deciding source; 2008 'Yulu' qualification chapter; 2009 'Le quatrième ton du yulu', JALL 30) via HAL's file URLs with a non-browser user readers (HAL now serves an Anubis bot challenge to browser UAs; the Internet Archive was offline). Boyeldieu 2007 MS p. 7 verbatim confirms the catalog quote ('Yulu does not seem to have any kind of stress or prosodic feature that clearly marks word boundaries'). Boyeldieu 2009 §2 (MS p. 2) and 2008 §1.2 add a refinement: lexical units contrast one 'intense' syllable (seven vowel qualities x length) with 'non-intense' syllables where all vowel contrasts neutralise to ə (canonical CVCə, CəCVCə, VCə; polysyllables end in a non-intense syllable), and the tone system has four level heights. This is a vowel-reduction prominence, not accent, so the catalog's 'tonal' coding stands; recommend adding Boyeldieu 2009 §2 as a supporting/refining source. Gabjanda 1976 thesis (held by the project from the earlier reading) contains no Yulu stress statement beyond the accent-vs-tone framework note.

new_statements.translation: The meaningful units of Yulu are generally characterised by the syntagmatic contrast of one 'intense' syllable – in which seven vowel qualities, doubled by a length correlation, are opposed – with one (or more) 'non-intense' syllable(s) – in which all vowel oppositions are neutralised in a single archiphoneme ə. [...] Polysyllables are thus generally characterised by a non-intense final syllable. [...] Yulu distinguishes four fixed (or 'level') tone heights.
new_statements.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 2009. Le quatrième ton du yulu. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 30: 197-234. HAL author MS halshs-00348143 (https://shs.hal.science/halshs-00348143/file/Yulu_4e_ton.pdf)
new_statements.locator: HAL MS §2 'Segments et formes canoniques', MS p. 2 (PDF pp. 3-4; the text layer) and §3 'Tons', MS p. 3 (the text layer)
new_statements.reading: First-hand phonological description by the language's principal describer. Yulu is a four-height tone language (3 high / 2 mid / 1 low / 0 extra-low, with the fourth partly a depressor split). Word-level prominence is expressed not as stress but as a vowel-quality asymmetry: each lexical unit has one 'intense' syllable carrying a full vowel (7 qualities x length), all other syllables reduced to schwa; canonical forms VCə, CVCə (majority), CəCVCə, CVCəCVCə, so the full-vowel syllable is the penult in the commonest shapes. Boyeldieu never calls this stress, and in 2007 (p. 7, verified verbatim in, PDF p. 8) states that Yulu 'does not seem to have any kind of stress or prosodic feature that clearly marks word boundaries'. So the catalog's classification 'tonal' is confirmed; the 2009 passage refines it (intense vs non-intense syllable = vowel-reduction prominence, not accent). Gabjanda 1976 (St Andrews PhD, held by the project) adds only the Mulderian accent-vs-tone theory passage and 'As for Yulu, distinctive para-phonotactic features [tones] are the most important' (printed p. 188); no Yulu stress statement.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction. Refinement only: the 2009 passage is a segmental/phonotactic description (full-vowel 'intense' nucleus vs schwa 'non-intense' nucleus), never framed as accent; the intense syllable is the penult in the majority VCə/CVCə/CəCVCə shapes, but reduplicated expressives CVCəCVCə carry two intense syllables and non-verbal lexemes drop the final schwa before pause ('forme réduite'), so it is not a culminative word-stress statement. Catalog stays 'tonal' with Boyeldieu 2007 p.7 as the deciding (only explicit) stress statement; 2009 §2 and 2008 §1.2 go in as supporting notes.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tonal classification and with the existing Boyeldieu 2007/2009 statements (no stress, tone-only word prosody). It adds an explicit accent-vs-tone framing in which tone is said to be the important para-phonotactic feature for Yulu, and an independent 1975 instrumental tone analysis. Its tone inventory (3 distinctive tones: level/rising/falling, from 4 phonetic levels) differs from Boyeldieu 2009's four level tone heights (3/2/1/0), but that is a tonal-analysis difference, not a stress claim. It also treats Yulu words as monosyllabic, whereas Boyeldieu 2009 gives CVCə etc. with a schwa syllable; again not a stress claim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gabjanda never states a word-stress or accent rule for Yulu. In his Mulderian framework 'accent' (contrastive para-phonotactic feature) and 'tone' (distinctive) are the two prosodic types; for Yulu he says the distinctive type (tone) is 'the most important' and analyses only tone: four phonetic pitch levels (High, Semi-High/Mid, Low-Mid, Low; 'confirmed by mingograms', p. 189) reduced to three distinctive tones, Tone I high level, Tone II rising, Tone III falling, established by minimal pairs such as /kad/ 'a person' vs 'salt' vs 'a donkey' (pp. 190-192). In the phonotactics chapter he treats the syllable as coinciding with the distributional unit and Yulu as 'monosyllabic and isolating' after Tucker 1940 (printed p. 163), so no polysyllabic word domain for stress is ever set up. The only 'stress' tokens in the Yulu-descriptive part are the Tucker & Bryan heading list ('phonetic, tone and stress', p. 148 region) and 'connotative stress' as a realizational feature distinguished from accent in the theory footnote (p. 33).
new_statements.exceptions: none; no stress rule is given so no exceptions
new_statements.identity_note: Gabjanda 1976 is by a native speaker (recordings made at SOAS in 1975), variety not named beyond 'Yulu'; Boyeldieu's work is on Yulu of the northern Central African Republic. No dialect distinction bears on the stress question.
